story.title: Pope Leo XIV Makes History as First Pontiff to Vote in a U.S. Election
story.summary: Pope Leo XIV has become the first pope in history to vote in a U.S. election, casting a mail-in ballot for the upcoming midterm elections. The Vatican confirmed that the Chicago-born pontiff exercised his right as a U.S. citizen by submitting his vote from Vatican City. The specific details of his ballot, including his choice of candidates, have not been disclosed.

explore_lenses.label: How could he vote from Vatican City?
explore_lenses.title: U.S. citizenship and Illinois residency govern
explore_lenses.summary: Leo’s location in Vatican City does not itself bar voting: overseas U.S. citizens can use absentee procedures for federal elections, while Illinois law sets the relevant state residency and registration rules.

claims.text: The Holy See Press Office confirmed that Leo submitted a mail-in ballot in Chicago as a U.S. citizen and described voting as his long-standing civic practice.
Federal law requires states to allow qualifying overseas U.S. citizens to register and vote by absentee ballot in elections for federal office; state law determines voting-residence eligibility.
Illinois law permits U.S. citizens temporarily outside the United States who are otherwise qualified to register and vote by mail through the election authority for their county of residence.
Will County’s chief of staff told the Chicago Sun-Times that Robert Francis Prevost, registered at a New Lenox address, requested a vote-by-mail ballot on October 3, 2026.

explore_lenses.label: Can the public learn whom Leo supported?
explore_lenses.title: No candidate choice has been disclosed
explore_lenses.summary: The public can learn some administrative facts about a mail ballot, but Illinois procedures are designed to keep the voter’s selections secret. Past primary-ballot requests do not reveal how he voted in a general election.

claims.text: The Holy See’s statement confirms participation but does not name any candidate, party, ballot measure, or voting choice.
Illinois vote-by-mail certifications require voters to attest that they personally marked the ballot in secret, and election law provides for ballots to be retained unopened before counting.

Illinois State Board of Elections spokesman Matt Dietrich said Illinois voters do not register by party and may choose a party’s ballot in a primary; the Sun-Times reported Prevost previously participated in both Democratic and Republican primaries.
A ballot being submitted does not by itself establish that it has been accepted and counted: Illinois officials compare the return-envelope signature and assess voter qualification before counting.

explore_lenses.label: Does Leo’s ballot endorse a U.S. party?
explore_lenses.title: The Vatican frames it as civic participation
explore_lenses.summary: The documented Vatican position is an endorsement of citizens’ participation in democratic processes, not an announced endorsement of a U.S. party or candidate.

claims.text: The Holy See Press Office said Leo believes citizens have both a right and a duty to participate in democratic processes.

The Vatican also said Leo had voted whenever eligible during his years living in Peru, presenting the Illinois ballot as part of an established personal practice rather than a new U.S.-election intervention.

The Chicago Sun-Times reported that the ballot includes the Illinois Senate, gubernatorial, judicial, and county contests, but neither the Vatican nor election officials disclosed Leo’s positions in any of them.

story_report.summary: Pope Leo XIV has become the first pope to vote in a U.S. election after the Holy See confirmed that he submitted a mail-in ballot in Chicago for the midterm elections as a U.S. citizen. The Vatican described voting as a long-standing civic practice for Leo, who it said believes citizens have both a right and duty to participate in democratic processes. The submission places a sitting pontiff in the U.S. electoral process for the first time, although submission alone does not establish that a ballot has been accepted and counted.

sections.heading: Illinois Rules Govern Leo’s Ballot
sections.body: Federal law requires states to provide qualifying overseas U.S. citizens a means to register and vote by absentee ballot in federal elections, while state law determines voting-residence eligibility. Illinois permits otherwise qualified U.S. citizens temporarily outside the country to register and vote by mail through the election authority in their county of residence. Will County’s chief of staff told the Chicago Sun-Times that Robert Francis Prevost, registered at a New Lenox address, requested a vote-by-mail ballot on Oct. 3, 2026.

sections.heading: Leo XIV’s Choices Remain Secret
sections.body: Neither the Holy See nor election officials disclosed any candidate, party, ballot measure or position selected by Leo. Illinois vote-by-mail rules require voters to attest that they personally marked their ballot in secret, and ballots are retained unopened before counting. County officials must compare the return-envelope signature and assess voter qualification before a returned ballot is counted; Illinois voters also do not register by party, according to the state board of elections spokesman cited by the Sun-Times.

related_stories.title: Netanyahu Accused of Smearing Arab Parties After Election Loss
related_stories.summary: Following the recent elections, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has been accused of using smear tactics against Arab Israeli parties, alleging they received foreign support to 'steal' the election. His coalition lost its parliamentary majority, prompting calls for investigations into alleged vote buying. As opposition parties begin coalition negotiations, Netanyahu's claims have sparked accusations of attempting to delegitimize the election results.

related_stories.title: Humanitarian Evacuations Begin in Oleshky Amid Severe Shortages
related_stories.summary: Evacuations of residents from Oleshky, a Russian-occupied town in southern Ukraine, commenced on October 30 as part of a joint relief operation involving both sides. This marks the first such operation in nearly five years of conflict. The area has faced dire food and medical shortages, prompting the urgent need for humanitarian assistance.
